title: Who Keeps the Water Out?
proposition: A floating house is only as independent as its mooring, its service connections and the institutions maintaining the water around it.
question: What changes when water becomes a condition around which everyday urban life is organised?
opening: Seventeen days of research in the Netherlands, within my SOM Foundation Fellowship, became a study of connections across scales: between a dwelling and its mooring, a street and its drainage, a public square and its storage capacity, a polder and its operating institutions. The journey is documented in Living with Water, an interactive field atlas. This essay draws out the architectural argument that links its individual places.
credit:
Research and synthesis · Hao Chang · SOM Foundation Fellow
Field research in the Netherlands · September 2026 · 17 days

sections.title: Defence and coexistence belong to the same system.
paragraphs: The familiar account of Dutch water management begins with the ability to exclude water. The field enquiry broadens the frame to include control, storage, accommodation and everyday occupation. These are overlapping strategies, not a simple historical progression in which one supersedes another. A floating neighbourhood still depends on regulated water levels, utilities and territorial protection.

The question for architecture is consequently not which single technology represents the future. It is how different capacities are connected, who can rely on them and what happens when one part is under stress. A basin that stores rainfall and a jetty that carries services are small spatial interfaces within much larger agreements.

sections.title: From the impressive object to the ordinary connection
paragraphs: De Urbanisten’s Benthemplein offers a useful comparative method: follow runoff through a public place and examine how hydraulic work coincides with daily occupation. I extend that reading from the square to canals, jetties and regional defences. The point is to draw dependencies, including those outside the photograph. A basin can be visible while its maintenance budget remains invisible. [N4]

Across the field atlas, I distinguish three conditions: a space that excludes water, a space designed to receive it temporarily, and an inhabited structure that moves with it. They cannot be ranked on a single scale of innovation. Each distributes risk differently. A floating dwelling still needs a stable point of access; a floodable square needs a route that remains usable when its basin is occupied; a barrier shifts attention to decisions about closure and reopening.

This produces a more demanding question than whether a place “lives with water”: which relationship is allowed to change, and which must be kept dependable? The answer is often a small junction between systems. The gangway, threshold, inlet and service connection are therefore central research objects, rather than minor details that follow the masterplan.

sections.title: Infrastructure extends beyond the visible object.
paragraphs: Kinderdijk, its pumping landscape and the Maeslantkering make very different forms of infrastructure visible. Read together, they shift attention from a recognisable object toward levels, connections, maintenance and coordinated operation. The atlas includes the Wisboomgemaal and Parksluizen because smaller operating components matter alongside celebrated structures.

A landscape can appear calm precisely because it is actively managed. The architectural lesson is to ask what makes that apparent stability possible. Drawings should record supply, servicing and responsibility as carefully as they record a building’s silhouette. The field account does not imply that every operating sequence was witnessed or that a visit can establish long-term performance.

sections.title: The canal is an urban section.
paragraphs: At Utrecht’s Oudegracht, water, lower wharf, cellar, street and building form an unusually legible vertical arrangement. The municipality’s historical reconstructions show how tunnels and wharf cellars developed over time. The edge is therefore an evolving connection between movement, storage and occupation, rather than a single boundary drawn on a plan. [N1]

Amsterdam’s Canal Ring and Delft’s waterways extend the enquiry to the scale of the city. For design, the transferable question is how a water system establishes addresses and thresholds: where a door meets a quay, how a bridge reconnects streets, or how servicing can coexist with a place to linger. The section makes these relationships available for comparison.

sections.title: A neighbourhood needs more than buoyancy.
paragraphs: Waterbuurt West is useful because it turns flotation into a problem of urban organisation. Rohmer’s project documentation describes shared jetties, flexible services, access and the separation of cars from the waterside circulation system. What appears as an individual floating house is supported by a collective framework. [N2]

Schoonschip adds a resident-led development model and shared infrastructure to this reading. Its jetty connects homes while organising services and social contact. The comparison shifts the question from whether a building can float to whether the surrounding system can support affordable, accessible and maintainable everyday life. [N3]

sections.title: The jetty is a collective agreement
paragraphs: Reading a floating neighbourhood as a collection of houses conceals the shared work carried by its access structure. I use a dependency register to connect a spatial component with an everyday need, a possible failure and a responsible actor. This is an analytical proposal for comparing the documented cases; it is not an audit of their actual service performance.

The distinction also changes how affordability should be investigated. Purchase cost alone cannot describe the burden of a waterside home. Repair access, shared charges, insurance and the ability to remain during servicing can determine who can sustain occupation. The field material does not establish those costs, but it identifies the questions that a design comparison would otherwise omit.

sections.title: Storage can become a public room.
paragraphs: At Benthemplein, De Urbanisten combine stormwater storage with public space. Different basin depths and visible runoff routes make changing conditions part of the square’s spatial organisation. The project was shaped through workshops with neighbouring users, placing participation alongside the hydraulic design. [N4]

This produces a precise design question: can the same space remain useful under more than one environmental condition? Its public value cannot be judged only when the basins are empty, nor its hydraulic role only during a storm. The design must make transitions understandable and support care between events. That question also returns to the paired seasonal sections of the Jakarta proposal.

sections.title: Institutions are part of the field.
paragraphs: The field atlas includes exchanges at MVRDV, PosadMaxwan and TU Delft. I place these visits beside the built cases because infrastructure is also produced through professional and institutional decisions. The research question is how a drawing becomes a brief, a funded project and an arrangement that can be maintained.

The interpretive value lies in connecting those stages, rather than assigning unrecorded statements to the people encountered. For each case, the next layer of research would identify who commissions, operates, repairs and evaluates the system. These roles can be distributed among several organisations even when the architecture appears continuous.

sections.title: What travels from Rotterdam to Jakarta?
paragraphs: A useful transfer preserves the question while changing the answer. Benthemplein suggests comparing public use before, during and after a water event. It does not imply that an equivalent basin belongs beneath a Jakarta viaduct. The rainfall regime, contaminated water, available ground, tenure and maintenance arrangements have to be reconsidered at the receiving site.

For the Jakarta proposal, the transferable instrument is a paired drawing with an additional recovery state. The test is whether refuge, access and sanitation remain connected when routine occupation is interrupted. Dutch fieldwork therefore sharpens the design brief without making the Netherlands a universal destination toward which other water cultures must progress.

sections.title: Design for a capacity to change.
paragraphs: The strongest lesson is not that Dutch technologies can be copied into every flood-prone city. Land tenure, finance, governance and hydrology differ. Transfer should begin with a question about relationships: how to preserve access, share services, retain public space and organise responsibility while environmental conditions change.

For my design work, this means beginning with water and collective systems before treating the building as an autonomous object. A resilient spatial framework should make room for maintenance, uncertain conditions and different forms of occupation. The atlas remains the place to examine individual cases, published drawings and the distinction between field records and additional research sites.
sections.statement: Design the relationships that allow a place to keep working as water conditions change.

title: The Trail Has to Earn Its Keep
proposition: A restored path can remain economically peripheral. The architectural question is what gives residents a recurring reason to use and maintain the territory around it.
question: How can architecture help a historic route sustain contemporary rural life?
opening: In April 2026, I joined the Tsinghua University–Politecnico di Torino field investigation in Valle d’Aosta. The Italian work formed a counterpart to research along the Tea Horse Trail in Yunnan. It reframed the route as a way to read connections among settlements, production, landscape and services, with architecture operating between those scales.
credit:
Field research and comparative synthesis · Hao Chang
Tsinghua University / Politecnico di Torino · April 2026
Joint programme: Martijn de Geus, Roberto Dini, Lidia Preti and Yi Shen

sections.title: Ancient trails as contemporary territory.
paragraphs: The joint programme connected the Tea Horse Trail and Via Francigena through the question of rural reactivation. The Alpine investigation included Aosta, Courmayeur, Saint-Rhémy-en-Bosses, Étroubles, Saint-Oyen and the Great St Bernard Pass. Encounters with local administrations, stakeholders and craftspeople placed everyday inhabitation within the research frame. [I1]

The comparison begins with a distinction: conserving the physical route and sustaining its surrounding territory are related but different tasks. A path may remain visible even as the services, livelihoods and social relationships that once supported it change. Architecture must therefore ask what makes passage useful to the places through which it passes.
sections.caption: Valle d’Aosta route context · Map reproduced in the graduation research presentation. A territorial reference, not a GPS track of the field itinerary.

sections.title: Walking as a method of reading relationships.
paragraphs: Slow movement makes distance, slope and thresholds part of architectural observation. A settlement is encountered through its approaches, service spaces, productive edges and places to stop. The method is to relate these local conditions to the wider network: a building’s capacity for reuse depends partly on what can reach it, who needs it and which activities can persist around it.

This reading does not treat a scenic view as evidence of a functioning rural economy. Photographs and route maps show spatial relations; questions about ownership, seasonal occupation or economic viability require other forms of enquiry. Keeping those forms of evidence distinct prevents a field essay from turning an attractive landscape into an uncomplicated model.

sections.title: Walk the service route as well as the visitor route
paragraphs: The joint research programme, with Roberto Dini, Lidia Preti, Martijn de Geus and Yi Shen, provides a comparative frame in which Alpine routes are examined through contemporary rural life. I use that frame to move from a scenic itinerary toward a transect of work: arrival, supply, making, storage, exchange and departure. This is the method developed in this essay, rather than a quotation of a participant’s position. [I1]

Walking reveals the effort between destinations. A map can place two buildings close together while a steep approach, a closed gate or a loading requirement makes their practical relation difficult. The relevant section therefore includes the service edge and the stopping place, not only the panorama. The same journey should be read from the position of someone carrying supplies and someone visiting without a burden.

That distinction is especially useful when examining reuse. An empty room is not automatically available capacity: it may be poorly connected to the activity expected to support it. The field observations establish physical questions. Interviews with operators and recurring seasonal records would be needed to establish whether the proposed connection is viable.

sections.title: Production gives the route another reason to be used.
paragraphs: The research presentation places the Via Francigena beside food-producing workshops and spaces of storage. These encounters matter because production is both a livelihood and a way for visitors to understand a territory. The stopping place becomes an interface between movement and work rather than merely an amenity added to a tourist itinerary.

The architectural consequence is a network question: where can paths, workshops, shared rooms and rest facilities reinforce one another? In Yunnan, this returns as the relationship between tea production, the ancient garden and accommodation. The comparison concerns how activities connect; it does not propose transferring Alpine forms into the tea landscape.
sections.caption: Productive spaces along the Alpine enquiry · Images documented in the graduation presentation connect local food production with the route; original individual photographer credits were not recorded in the slide.

sections.title: The missing drawing is a working calendar
paragraphs: Food production brings different durations into the trail. Making, maturing, storing, selling and visiting do not occupy the same hours or seasons. A room serving more than one of these activities needs a negotiated timetable as much as a flexible plan. Public access may be appropriate at the edge of production while remaining incompatible with a clean work zone or a delivery period.

I propose reading a stopping place against three calendars: the resident’s ordinary week, the production cycle and the visitor season. Where all three coincide, shared facilities may have a strong everyday base. Where only the visitor season activates a building, the project risks adding another maintenance obligation to a territory with intermittent revenue. The observations do not yet establish an operating balance; the calendar is the next evidence needed to test it.

This makes modest interventions consequential. A covered waiting place, accessible store or shared washing facility may support an existing cycle more reliably than a new exhibition room. Architectural value can be assessed through the work made easier and the relationships kept in use, alongside the experience offered to a visitor.

sections.title: Tourism is one condition of inhabitation.
paragraphs: Courmayeur complicates a simple narrative of rural decline. A territory can attract substantial visitor activity while still raising questions about housing, services and the continuity of permanent community life. Here these are research questions, not a claim that the field visit established household displacement or measured seasonal vacancy.

For architecture, the useful distinction is between an intervention that draws attention to a place and one that expands its capacity to be lived in. Reuse, everyday services and shared facilities deserve to be considered alongside visitor accommodation. Their value may be less spectacular but more continuous.

sections.title: Attention is not the same as livelihood
paragraphs: Tourism can give a workshop an audience while changing what it makes, when it opens and whose needs organise the space. The productive encounter can become a staged demonstration. This is a tension to examine, not an accusation about the visited businesses. A comparative study should ask whether visitors supplement an existing economy or gradually become its condition of survival.

A counterfactual makes the distinction concrete: if visitor numbers fell for a season, which part of the proposed intervention would still be useful to residents? The answer may identify the most durable element of the brief. It also challenges the assumption that a stronger visual identity is sufficient to reactivate a rural place. A recognisable destination and an inhabitable territory are different achievements.

sections.title: From Yunnan to the Alps.
paragraphs: The ICOMOS Cultural Routes Charter helps situate routes within reciprocal exchange and connected heritage. The two territories, however, remain historically and institutionally different. Comparison is productive when it reveals a common question while preserving those differences. [I3]

sections.title: Architecture after the fieldwork.
paragraphs: The programme moved from investigation to discussion and exhibition at Castello del Valentino, Turin, on 14 April 2026. This dissemination stage brought student work from the two institutions into one comparative setting. [I2]

My architectural position is to start with relationships that already give a territory its life: production, access, care and recurring use. A new intervention should strengthen selected connections within that system. The Gaoligong project tests this through different degrees of presence, from more collective facilities near accessible ground to lighter structures along the mountain route.

title: A Working Mountain
proposition: The ancient trail will not regain continuity through scenery alone. Its future depends on the work, access and care that give people reasons to return.
question: How can architecture reconnect a fragmented historic trail, local production and ecological experience without turning the landscape into another object of development?
opening: The Yongchang Trail is read here as a territorial system rather than an isolated heritage route. At Fenglaoye Ancient Tea Garden, its continuity depends on the working relationships between the path, tea production and the forest. The architectural task is to repair those relationships with a degree of intervention that changes across the site.
credit:
Individual graduation research and design · Hao Chang · Tsinghua University, 2026
Instructor: Martijn de Geus · Comparative research with Politecnico di Torino

sections.title: A route interrupted; a productive landscape still present.
paragraphs: The thesis locates Dahaoping on the Yongchang section of the Southern Silk Road. It traces the marginalisation of the mountain trail following the opening of the Baoshan–Tengchong road in 1952. Milestones, beacon towers and other dispersed traces remain, but their former network of movement and exchange has weakened. This is a break in relationships as much as a break in the path.

At Fenglaoye, the tea factory, old tea garden and existing accommodation are poorly connected in movement and visibility. Tea production nevertheless supplies a contemporary reason to use and care for this inherited landscape. The enquiry asks how productive continuity might sustain heritage without making tourism its only source of value.
sections.caption: 01 / Trail and dispersed heritage traces. Extracted from Hao Chang’s graduation presentation, PDF p. 4. The regional map establishes the research territory; it is not a cadastral survey.

sections.title: The factory is an anchor, not a backdrop
paragraphs: Xu Tiantian’s Brown Sugar Factory in Songyang is a useful methodological comparison because an existing productive activity gives the architectural brief its substance. DnA describes production, village use and public observation within a shared building. I take from this the question of what an intervention enables people to keep doing, rather than borrowing its appearance. [G5]

At Fenglaoye, the tea factory should therefore be read as an operating anchor. The relation between factory, garden and accommodation is not merely a sequence of visitor experiences. It also concerns the movement of people and material, the distinction between work and leisure, and the attention demanded by cultivation. A visitor path is successful only if it can meet these activities without turning every productive space into a performance.

The comparison has a limit. A compact workshop and a dispersed mountain landscape distribute access and maintenance differently. Here, the connecting path itself is an extensive piece of infrastructure. The research must ask whether each new destination justifies the route, servicing and labour required to keep it open.

sections.title: From a scenic itinerary to a working network.
paragraphs: Comparative fieldwork along the Via Francigena, undertaken with Politecnico di Torino, provided a different way of understanding a route. The graduation account describes food-producing workshops and stopping places as both economic activities and cultural encounters. Their significance lies in the connection between passage and production, rather than a repeated architectural style.

Transferred to Yunnan, this becomes a proposition to connect walking, ecological study and tea-making. The comparison suggests a network of exchanges, not a resort detached from its surroundings. Governance, land tenure and local economic conditions differ between the two contexts; the Italian observations do not demonstrate that the same operating model will work in Dahaoping.

The ICOMOS Cultural Routes Charter provides a wider frame for reading routes through exchange and connected heritage, while the joint Alpine programme extends that question to rural inhabitation. Neither requires the two landscapes to share the same architectural form. [G3] [G4]

sections.title: Map sensitivity before assigning programme.
paragraphs: The site study combines GIS elevation and slope analysis, sightlines, vegetation mapping, existing facilities and access constraints. The thesis distinguishes the flatter northern ground from steeper southern tea woodland. Mapped trees and openings inform setbacks and possible footprints; views guide orientation, while unloading and transport requirements determine where more intensive activity can be accommodated.

Read together, these layers identify a gradient of intervention. The research finding is not simply that buildings should be small. Public use, privacy, access and ecological sensitivity require different degrees of presence in different parts of the landscape.

sections.title: A small cabin can have a large territorial footprint
paragraphs: The footprint shown in plan is only one part of disturbance. Bringing components to a slope, installing foundations, supplying water, removing waste and replacing a failed element all require movement across the site. Several small buildings may distribute these demands over a larger area than a carefully located shared facility. “Small” is consequently an insufficient environmental criterion.

I read the proposal through a disturbance chain: access, installation, occupation, maintenance and eventual removal. The northern ground can accommodate more collective activity because access and terrain differ from the southern tea woodland. That is a conditional spatial argument, not a claim that the resulting construction is impact-free. Mapped trees need root-zone assessment; point foundations still require a site-specific installation strategy.

The same analysis produces a test for the network. If a distant unit cannot be serviced without repeatedly damaging a path or increasing vehicle access, its programme should be reduced, relocated or omitted. The right to leave a location unbuilt belongs inside the design method, rather than appearing only as an environmental qualification after the layout is fixed.

sections.title: Architectural acupuncture, from network to joint.
paragraphs: A continuous walking sequence reconnects the factory, garden and dispersed activities. Public reception acts as a threshold, while small shelters and shared facilities supply places to stop. The network turns the path into an inhabited sequence without requiring a continuous building frontage.

At the construction scale, point foundations, raised floors and small-module dry assembly test how the ground can remain more continuous beneath the intervention. The cabin studies combine timber members, bracing and replaceable connections; shared bathing facilities introduce a proposed local water-treatment cycle. These are architectural hypotheses about reduced disturbance and maintenance, not measured ecological outcomes.
sections.caption: 03 / Cabin construction study. Hao Chang, graduation presentation, PDF p. 52. Point supports and an elevated floor translate site sensitivity into a construction strategy.

sections.title: Where the public route stops
paragraphs: A connected landscape does not require universal access to every space. The factory, shared reception, accommodation and bathing facilities have different relationships to work, privacy and service. The design research asks where a common route should branch, where a threshold should slow movement and where a view can replace physical entry.

This differentiates continuity from exposure. A visitor can understand tea production without entering a work area; a guest can be connected to a shared facility without the room becoming part of a public promenade. The network is strongest when it makes these relationships readable. Its social success would depend on an operating agreement that protects production and allocates the benefits and costs of visitor use.

sections.title: Continuity must also be operational.
paragraphs: The thesis identifies further work on microclimate, carbon accounting and wet-season wastewater maintenance. Root-zone protection, foundation installation, habitat disturbance and disassembly would need specialist assessment. Claims of “zero disturbance” or “zero pollution” are therefore treated here as ambitions rather than established results.

The unresolved social question is equally important: who operates the network, who benefits from tea-related tourism, and how can local production retain agency? The aim is not to restore the trail to what it was, but to rebuild the relationships that allow it to remain alive.

title: Planting Factories, Moving Villages
proposition: A land-use map can show where a factory or a house stands while leaving out the networks and collective rights that make its location matter.
question: What do local terms make visible where the city and countryside coexist?
opening: Two glossary entries approach Taiwan’s rurban territories through language. 農地種工廠 names an incremental process of industrialisation on farmland. Niyaro’ describes community through collective territory and relations rather than rural location alone. Read together, the terms ask how architecture can respond to mixed territories without reducing them to an incomplete version of either city or countryside.
credit:
Glossary essays and territorial reading · Hao Chang · 2026
Developed for the Glossary of Rurbanity open call, Harvard GSD
“Planting Factories on Farmland” · Selected contribution; companion entry: Niyaro’

sections.title: Naming the rurban interface.
paragraphs: The Glossary of Rurbanity forms part of Harvard GSD’s Carrots and Sticks: Incentives Shaping the “Rurban” Interface conference, held on 11 September 2026. The call brings keywords, short essays and images into a comparative discussion of how urban and rural conditions are named in different languages. [R1]

The value of a glossary is not simply translation. A word can indicate what must be explained: a process, a shared territory, a mode of production or an institutional mismatch. These entries move from meaning to spatial condition and then to a design question.

sections.title: Follow the relation that the category cannot contain
paragraphs: AMO’s Countryside research treats nonurban territory as a site of contemporary transformation, including production, technology and political decisions. It provides a useful invitation to investigate what a familiar category leaves out. The local meanings of 農地種工廠 and Niyaro’ come from their own scholarship and communities, however; an international exhibition cannot define them. [R10]

My glossary method has four steps. Identify what the term names; establish the scale at which it operates; trace the relations extending beyond that scale; then ask what a conventional plan would fail to protect. The industrial parcel extends through subcontracting, roads and water. The dwelling extends through cultivation, kinship, ritual and shared territory. Each word therefore changes the unit of analysis.

This is why the entries remain separate. A factory operating on farmland and an Indigenous community facing relocation cannot be placed on one ladder from informal to formal. Their histories, powers and claims differ. The comparison is about the limits of spatial categories, not an equivalence between the groups who occupy them.

sections.title: 農地種工廠 — Planting Factories on Farmland.
paragraphs: Nóngdì zhòng gōngchǎng names a process rather than just a land-use type. Factories are “planted” parcel by parcel while fields, irrigation channels, rural roads and settlements remain legible. Wu’s research distinguishes this extended urbanisation from an earlier condition in which rural industry drew on a countryside labour pool: peripheral farmland becomes a land pool as production moves outward. [R2]

Across the Taichung–Changhua belt, networks of small firms and subcontractors meet agricultural parcels and uneven regulation. Buck examines the construction and decentralisation of Taiwan’s industrial networks; Lin and Su’s Dingfanpo study brings the environmental and distributive conflicts of agricultural-industrial coexistence into focus. [R3] [R4]
sections.caption: Dingfanpo, Lukang · Factories among agricultural parcels. Photograph: Tsai Chia-yang / Changhua Environmental Protection Union, 2016. Source: CEPU / Citizens of the Earth, Taiwan.

sections.title: A design field between parcels.
paragraphs: Regulatory responses include pathways for eligible older unregistered factories under Taiwan’s Factory Management and Counseling Act. Changhua’s June 2026 planning review addresses designated specific-factory zones. These mechanisms organise registration and land-use review; they do not by themselves resolve every spatial relationship within a mixed territory. [R5] [R6]

The unresolved design field lies between parcels: irrigation and drainage, road access, fire safety, pollution control and agricultural continuity. The question is how to retrofit these shared systems without making either the expulsion of industry or wholesale conversion of farmland the only imaginable response.
sections.caption: Parcel structure in Dingfanpo · Diagram by Hao Chang, 2026, based on the Taiwan Ministry of Agriculture’s Agricultural and Farmland Resources Inventory Map.

sections.title: The boundary of ownership is not the boundary of impact
paragraphs: A parcel-by-parcel response can make individual sites administratively legible while leaving the shared landscape fragmented. Water crosses property lines; delivery vehicles use common roads; agricultural work depends on connections that an isolated building permit cannot represent. The research unit must therefore include the path of a burden, as well as the boundary of the activity producing it.

For a future spatial study, I would overlay the production network with drainage, cultivated land, freight access and sensitive neighbouring uses. The purpose would be to identify where an individual improvement is inadequate and a collective intervention becomes necessary. No pollution measurements or completed environmental assessment are claimed here. The glossary establishes why those measurements must be related spatially.

That distinction prevents an architectural proposal from treating a tidier facade or a landscaped setback as resolution. A change should be judged against the relation it repairs: whether it separates conflicting movement, reduces exposure or maintains an agricultural connection. Otherwise visual improvement may conceal the same distribution of costs.

sections.title: Niyaro’ — Community beyond a rural location.
paragraphs: Niyaro’ is a Pangcah / ’Amis word for a village or community; it does not mean “peri-urban.” Huang’s account and Wu’s research on Xizhou help situate community through collective territory, kinship, work, ritual, shared space and self-organisation. Urban riverbank communities demonstrate why these relations cannot be reduced to distance from a metropolitan centre. [R7] [R8]

At Xizhou, on the Xindian River, cultivation, gathering and ritual life accompanied self-built housing. Flood-control and demolition pressure led to negotiation over a safer form of staying. The municipal account records the nearby rehousing of 34 households through a “333” self-help funding model and shared cultural facilities. [R9]
sections.caption: Xizhou / Cinemnemay after relocation · Thirty-four households at the metropolitan river edge. Image: New Taipei City Government, Water Resources Department, 2022.

sections.title: What must move with a house?
paragraphs: Relocation is more than moving dwelling units. If community is sustained through livelihood, ecology, collective space and ritual, then retaining a building count is an incomplete measure of continuity. The design question is what must move with the houses for a niyaro’ to remain a niyaro’.

This entry is a reading of published scholarship and public project documentation, not a claim to speak for Xizhou residents. Questions of cultural meaning and acceptable change require the community’s own authority. Architecture can make the spatial stakes visible without assuming that a plan settles them.

sections.title: A relocation plan needs a second inventory
paragraphs: The first inventory counts houses and facilities. The second records which relations depend on proximity: who shares cultivation, where collective preparation occurs, how a gathering moves between indoor and outdoor space, and how access to the river supports memory or livelihood. These are questions for community-led documentation, not a checklist an outside architect can complete alone.

The two inventories can disagree. A rehousing scheme may improve the dwelling while weakening an activity that had no dedicated room in the original settlement. Conversely, reproducing an old spatial arrangement without addressing risk can also fail its inhabitants. The design problem is to negotiate material improvement and collective continuity together, with the people concerned deciding which relations are indispensable.

sections.title: Two terms, different forms of continuity.
paragraphs: The two terms should not be collapsed into one generic category of informality. One traces industrialisation through farmland; the other names the continuing relations of an Indigenous community. Both expose a mismatch between a static spatial category and an active territorial process.

For design, the implication is to investigate the shared systems that sustain a place before prescribing a new identity for it. In one case those systems include irrigation, production and environmental burdens; in the other, collective space, cultural practice and the ability to remain. Language becomes an instrument for deciding what architecture must notice.

title: When the River Occupies the Street
proposition: Raising a floor protects a room. Keeping a neighbourhood habitable requires the route, the toilet, the supply point and the means to repair them to remain connected.
question: How can civic infrastructure learn from the everyday adaptations already practised in Kampung Melayu, allowing access, livelihood, care and collective life to continue as water levels change?
opening: Flood resilience begins with the routines that keep a neighbourhood functioning. Raising a floor, moving possessions, sharing shelter and maintaining access are spatial practices as well as acts of care. The research translates a reading of these practices into a framework that can change with the river.
credit:
Individual design research · Hao Chang · 2025
Instructor: Martijn de Geus · SOM China Fellowship recipient

sections.title: Three scales of an uneven water system.
paragraphs: At the metropolitan scale, the research notes connect flooding with land subsidence, groundwater dependence, urbanisation and drainage. At the river scale, the Ciliwung brings questions of water quality, settlement and access into contact. At the neighbourhood scale, Kampung Melayu exposes how a change in water level affects housing, work, sanitation and routes to shared services.

This macro–meso–micro reading prevents a single technical response from standing in for the whole problem. Protecting a building does not automatically protect its inhabitants’ livelihoods or their access to care. The framework therefore reads hydrological exposure together with social continuity.
sections.caption: 01 / Multi-scalar research framework. Hao Chang, Rising Tides, Resilient Lives portfolio. The matrix connects metropolitan water pressures, the river corridor and everyday neighbourhood needs.

sections.title: Adaptation is already spatial.
paragraphs: Research on informal adaptation in North Jakarta directs attention to the everyday knowledge and practices through which communities respond to flooding. This study uses that literature as a comparative lens for raised living spaces, protected storage, temporary access and mutual assistance. These are literature-informed design questions; they are not the results of a new household survey in Kampung Melayu. [J5] [J6]

The notes draw from different Jakarta contexts, including North Jakarta. Their transfer to Kampung Melayu must therefore remain a question for site-specific investigation. The architectural inference is to support existing capacities while addressing the points where individual adaptation cannot maintain a collective service.

headers: Practice described in the research notes
rows: Can routes change without becoming isolated?

sections.statement: Adaptation is not the return to a fixed normal. It is the capacity for everyday life to continue through change.

sections.title: Who has the capacity to adapt?
paragraphs: Kéré’s Atelier Gando makes skills and material experimentation part of architectural production. As a comparative method, this shifts attention from the finished component to who can make, maintain and alter it. The Jakarta proposal’s modular assembly must be tested on those terms: a component is not locally repairable simply because its diagram is simple. [J7]

The Friendship Centre by Kashef Chowdhury / URBANA offers another comparison. Its flood response is tied to the economics and spatial organisation of a specific institution. That prompts a cost-and-responsibility question here, rather than a recommendation to reproduce its embankment beside the Ciliwung. Moving water away from one site can change exposure elsewhere. [J8]

These comparisons expose a danger in celebrating informal resilience. The ability to keep adapting may depend on unpaid labour, spare space, social support and resources that households possess unequally. A shared refuge must reduce these burdens rather than assume an inexhaustible capacity to absorb them. Community participation is a design commitment to organise, not an achievement established by the unbuilt scheme.

sections.title: A stable datum, changing occupation.
paragraphs: Paired dry- and flood-season sections are the principal design test. The railway viaduct is read as a relatively stable spatial datum around which access and occupation can be reorganised. Keeping the frame constant makes it possible to compare what changes: thresholds, movement, storage and the relationship between public rooms and water.

The dry-season section accommodates markets, workshops, kitchens and shared space. Flood conditions shift parts of the system toward refuge, boat landings and relief. The finding is a design inference: continuity may depend on a durable support with adaptable use, rather than a return to an identical ground-level arrangement after every flood.
sections.caption: 02 / Dry-season section. Everyday civic uses establish the network that flood response will depend on. Hao Chang, portfolio.

sections.title: The third section: after the water recedes
paragraphs: The paired seasonal drawings show occupation before and during inundation. A third state is necessary to test recovery. A market that becomes a shelter must eventually become a market again; stored goods, deposited sediment, contaminated surfaces and interrupted services can delay that return. A dry floor alone does not establish that a room is ready for use.

I therefore read each shared space through a chain of dependencies. Who closes it, what remains accessible, where supplies are stored, who cleans it and what allows it to reopen? These are proposed evaluation questions, not a completed emergency plan. Their spatial implications are specific: separate clean storage from flood-contact areas, maintain a legible route between refuge and services, and leave access for repair.

sections.title: Water security extends beyond the flood event.
paragraphs: The proposal links roof-water collection, wastewater treatment and wetland buffers. This extends the study from flood avoidance to the relationship between clean supply, contaminated flows and the public landscape. Storage, treatment and overflow should be legible as distinct parts of a cycle, not collapsed into a claim that all water can be safely reused.

The spatial consequence is to place environmental infrastructure alongside daily civic use. Wetland edges and modular dwellings are studied as connected components of a river corridor; the section exposes their relationships while leaving treatment capacity and engineering performance open to verification.
sections.caption: 03 / Flood-season section. The architectural frame remains, while water levels, access and occupation change. A design scenario, not a measured flood simulation.

sections.title: A framework to test with residents.
paragraphs: The viaduct is a spatial reference, not an automatically available foundation or guaranteed safe datum. Structural independence, transport-authority requirements, clearance and maintenance access need to be resolved before the elevated public spine can be treated as feasible. Flood levels, water velocity and debris loads also require engineering evidence beyond the architectural sections.

A meaningful next stage would bring residents, service providers and the relevant authorities into a comparison of alternatives: improve existing local facilities, add a shared elevated route, or concentrate support at fewer accessible nodes. The proposal should be revised if its maintenance demands exceed the capacity of those expected to run it.

The argument is consequently about continuity rather than invulnerability. The Netherlands field enquiry extends the comparison by asking how spatial systems and operating responsibilities are connected. It supplies questions for Jakarta, not a ready-made institutional or technical answer.

title: Before the Curtain Rises
subtitle: The theatre as a public building during its non-performance hours
method: OMA / Rem Koolhaas and David Gianotten · Analyse programme, circulation and institutional thresholds
proposition: The theatre’s most public room may be the one that does not require a performance. The research begins with the hours when the auditorium is closed.
question: How can a theatre support independent everyday use while maintaining the acoustic, technical and access requirements of performance?
opening: Wudaokou brings university, workplace and residential rhythms into close proximity. The Condenser asks what a theatre can contribute to that mixture between scheduled events. Its research treats the building as an arrangement of programmes, routes and opening conditions. The design then tests that argument through a raised ground, shared foyers, stairs and a roof landscape.
credit:
Individual typological research and design · Hao Chang · Spring 2025
Tsinghua University · Large-scale Public Building Design Studio
Comparative readings extend the original project argument; they do not imply collaboration with the referenced practices.

sections.title: Start with the institution’s timetable
paragraphs: A conventional reading begins with auditorium capacity, stage requirements and the movement of a ticketed audience. Those remain essential. A second reading begins with the surrounding city: a student between classes, a worker on a break, a resident taking a walk. Their demand for somewhere to meet does not necessarily coincide with the programme inside the hall.

The original design argument identifies openness and shared use as responses to that mismatch. The sharper research question is how much of the building can remain useful without a ticket, a scheduled event or the expense of operating every performance space. The empty hours are not simply a programming failure; they reveal the limits of organising a civic building around a single institutional rhythm.

sections.title: Treat the programme as something to argue with
paragraphs: OMA’s account of the Taipei Performing Arts Center questions the standardised composition and public role of the contemporary theatre. The Public Loop, documented by the institution, provides a specific comparison for circulation that is not confined to the conventional audience sequence. I take these as research operations: challenge the inherited brief and examine who can enter which parts of the building. [T1] [T2]

The Condenser does not reproduce that project’s organisation. Its enquiry concerns the productive distance between enclosed performance rooms and a looser civic interior. The key drawing is a programme relationship diagram: which uses need isolation, which can share support, and which can invite unscheduled occupation?

Calling this a social condenser is only the beginning of the argument. Co-presence does not guarantee exchange. People can occupy the same building without a reason to meet, or be forced into contact they would prefer to avoid. The architecture needs places for encounter and places to withdraw, with enough distinction that neither use invalidates the other.

sections.title: Three publics, more than one route
paragraphs: I distinguish the ticketed audience, the everyday visitor and the people making the performance. They overlap, but their requirements are not interchangeable. The audience needs orientation and a coordinated arrival; an everyday visitor needs an intelligible place to go without entering the ticketed sequence; performers and technicians need dependable working access.

The distinction prevents openness from becoming a demand that every route be shared. Backstage privacy, equipment movement and acoustic separation are necessary parts of the institution. The research instead asks where selected adjacencies can make performance perceptible without interrupting its production. A view, a foyer or a shared edge can connect uses without merging their circulation.

sections.title: The stair is a room only if movement can continue
paragraphs: The design uses stairs at several scales, culminating in a gathering stair between levels three and four. This converts a change in level into a place for discussion, informal viewing and pause. Its value is not the visual drama of a crowded rendering. The test is whether someone can remain while someone else passes, and whether the gathering has a legible edge.

A sectional reading exposes the trade-off. More shared volume can increase contact while transmitting noise and making supervision harder. A roof destination can extend occupation while adding weather exposure and a dependence on vertical access. The architectural proposition must therefore be evaluated with parallel routes, acoustic boundaries and closure scenarios.

The current sections establish possible relationships. They do not certify egress, accessibility or acoustic performance. A subsequent iteration would test the same public sequence during an ordinary afternoon, an event arrival and an interval, retaining comparable routes so that congestion and conflicts become visible.
sections.caption: The Condenser · Long section. Hao Chang, 2025. The drawing tests relations between enclosed performance, shared circulation and the roof; it is a design proposal.

sections.title: Visibility is not permission
paragraphs: The blue and orange performance volumes and translucent polycarbonate envelope give occupation a presence after dark. They make the institution perceptible from outside and relate its different parts to the surrounding urban conditions. The research distinguishes this visual invitation from the ability to enter or use a space.

A transparent or luminous facade can advertise an activity that remains inaccessible. Conversely, a modest entrance can provide an effective public threshold if its destination and rules are clear. The envelope should therefore be read beside entry, signage and operating hours. The question is whether the building’s visible promise corresponds to an available form of use.
sections.caption: The Condenser · Exploded programme and circulation study. Hao Chang, 2025.

sections.title: A test without a show
paragraphs: The decisive scenario removes the performance. The auditoria are closed, technical work is limited and there is no audience to populate the foyer. Can the ground, stair and roof sequence still form a useful civic place? Which parts could operate independently, and which would require staffing or environmental systems disproportionate to their use?

This test makes shared space an accountable part of the brief. Independent access, a clear boundary to controlled rooms, places to sit and a feasible maintenance arrangement are more persuasive than a general claim of flexibility. If a proposed public area cannot remain open under these conditions, its public role should be described more narrowly.

The research produces criteria rather than proof of social transformation. The design page shows how the proposal arranges entrances, performance volumes, the gathering stair and roof. Those decisions can now be evaluated against a specific promise: a theatre that contributes to urban life before the curtain rises, with the limits of that promise made explicit.

title: After the Battery
proposition: An art museum enters a landscape built for concealment and command. Its task is to change how that ground is encountered without making its military history disappear.
question: How can architecture translate the layered spatial memory of a military landscape into contemporary cultural life without reconstructing a single past or erasing the traces between them?
opening: The military landscape is an arrangement of visibility, concealment, supply and movement. Ruins preserve parts of this arrangement; missing structures and altered ground also carry evidence. The museum study asks how another cultural use can enter that record without making its different moments appear complete or simultaneous.
credit:
Individual studio and design research · Hao Chang · 2024
Instructor: Li Xiaodong · Historical and conservation evidence credited separately below

sections.title: Read a palimpsest, not a single origin.
paragraphs: The fortress investigation distinguishes structures, construction phases, alterations and survival. Regional Ming–Zheng and Qing histories provide the wider coastal context; they should not be assigned indiscriminately to every surviving wall. Japanese-period construction and extension, postwar military use, abandonment and contemporary reuse form further layers. [P1]

The research method separates documentary history from visible fabric. A missing building is recorded as an absence, not filled in to produce a seamless historical image. This distinction matters because a museum route can otherwise turn a complicated military landscape into a simplified scene.
sections.caption: 01 / Historical and natural layers of the peninsula. Hao Chang, Erdai Art Museum portfolio. Historical chronology is read against the separately credited fortress investigation.

rows: Ming–Zheng and Qing coastal context; distinguish context from dating of fabric
Emplacements, shelter, additions and altered circulation
Reuse, loss, interruption and remaining traces
A legible new layer, without completing an imagined past

sections.title: Three systems within one ground.
paragraphs: The fortress investigation organises military architecture into combat, habitation and communication spaces. Read together with topography, these categories explain how commanding views coexist with concealed rooms and protected routes. Water collection, storage and filtration also make the site legible as an inhabited system rather than only a set of weapons positions. [P1]

This is a reading of a published survey, not a claim to have produced its measured drawings. The design research then asks which spatial relationships can continue: a route along a trench, an outlook from high ground, a sheltered threshold, or the relationship between an underground room and daylight.

rows: High ground, exposure and directed views
Can looking become reflection rather than surveillance?
What makes an interior inhabitable in this exposed landscape?
Can a cultural route preserve the legibility of the network?

sections.title: A new route is already an interpretation
paragraphs: Carlo Scarpa’s work at Castelvecchio brings the design of a museum into direct relation with the adaptation of a historic fortress. I use that relationship as a comparative question: how does a contemporary route disclose the inherited building, and where does the display apparatus become another layer to read? This is a method of close examination, not a vocabulary of details to reproduce. [P5]

At the Dashan battery, concealment and exposure were operational relationships. A trench protected movement; a high point extended a view; an enclosed chamber separated occupation from the weather and the horizon. Turning them into a cultural itinerary changes their purpose. The museum cannot claim to reveal an untouched truth simply by following an existing path.

The critical drawing is therefore a junction drawing. It should identify what survives, what has been removed, what is uncertain and what is proposed. A new handrail, floor, opening or lighting element should not blur that distinction. Legibility can be produced through a gap, a change of material or a different alignment, but the appropriate detail depends on verified fabric and conservation requirements.

sections.title: Preserve, reuse, translate.
paragraphs: Fu Chao-ching’s discussion of heritage translation distinguishes conserving fabric, reactivating use and interpreting inherited cultural relationships. It supplies a conceptual lens for this study, rather than a licence to remove inconvenient historical evidence. [P2]

In the museum proposal, preservation retains significant traces; adaptive reuse gives existing spaces another use; translation carries spatial relationships into new architecture. The three operations may meet within a single route, but they answer different questions. The museum becomes another historical layer, not a replacement for the military landscape.
sections.statement: Preservation is not the completion of the past. It is the careful addition of another layer.

sections.title: Do not complete every missing wall
paragraphs: An incomplete ruin can make time visible. Completing it to recover a coherent silhouette may remove precisely the evidence that distinguishes abandonment, alteration and loss. Conversely, leaving everything untouched can make a site inaccessible or accelerate damage. The useful opposition is not intervention versus non-intervention, but the purpose and reversibility of each action.

I distinguish three kinds of absence. A documented lost element can be interpreted without necessarily being reconstructed. An uncertain element should remain explicitly uncertain. A removal required by the new use must be justified as a contemporary decision. Recording these separately would allow the museum to show its own involvement in the history it presents.

This also gives the artwork an active role. The collection does not have to illustrate military chronology. Its juxtaposition with a buried room, a court or a distant sea view can open another register of attention. The curatorial sequence should nevertheless avoid turning the former battery into a neutral picturesque container in which its earlier uses are no longer readable.

sections.title: The section turns evidence into experience.
paragraphs: The design script begins at the former support area, then follows a sequence through partly buried galleries, reused emplacement spaces and a tunnel toward the southern sea view. Courts orient the interior toward the battery and supply indirect daylight. Changes of level and carefully framed views translate the existing ground into a sequence of encounters.

Different light conditions accompany different works in the Zhao Erdai collection. This is an architectural interpretation: compression, darkness, release and horizon propose ways of reading the site bodily. They do not claim to reproduce what its former occupants experienced.
sections.caption: 02 / Section through the proposed museum. New cultural space is inserted into the ground; the sequence of courts, galleries and sea views tests a contemporary reading of the inherited terrain.

sections.title: The visitor’s experience and the object’s conditions
paragraphs: The sequence of dark passage, court and horizon is compelling as an experience of the body. A collection, however, has another route: delivery, storage, handling, installation and conservation. These two itineraries need to meet selectively. The proposal’s section should be tested against both, especially where coastal exposure and changes of level make movement or environmental control more difficult.

Daylight is similarly double-sided. A framed view can orient a visitor while exposing an object to light that is inappropriate for its medium. The next iteration should separate the view offered to a person from the light reaching a work. The resulting architecture may depend on the depth and orientation of a threshold, rather than simply the size of an opening.

sections.title: Keep the archive open.
paragraphs: Conservation suitability cannot be established by a compelling section alone. Archaeological investigation, structural condition, coastal weathering, drainage and accessibility require further assessment. Water systems described in the investigation should be conserved or interpreted on the basis of their verified condition, not assumed to function unchanged.

The investigation and adaptive-reuse report remain independent evidence sources. The student proposal adds an interpretive argument to them; it does not replace a conservation plan or prove future visitor response. Its unresolved question is how to support new cultural life while allowing the site’s gaps and contradictions to remain visible.

title: The Right to Remain Unbuilt
proposition: A route can need better care without needing more architectural attention. Safety, sacred meaning and ecological disturbance must be evaluated separately before they are brought into one siting decision.
question: How can architectural infrastructure along the Mount Kailash kora be located, scaled and operated to meet essential needs without weakening its ritual sequence, sacred landscape and ecological integrity?
opening: The kora is at once a ritual sequence, a physically demanding journey and an ecological setting. The research brings landscape perception, facility evaluation and territorial conditions together to ask not only what is needed, but where architecture should keep its distance, adapt, retain or add as little as possible.
credit:
Collaborative studio research · Hao Chang & Mengzhe Lee · 2024
Instructor: Yue Cao · Hao’s portfolio role: research, modelling, renderings and diagrams

sections.title: From images to a landscape of attention.
paragraphs: The team’s December presentation and script document 1,729 geolocated social-media images. Kernel-density mapping identifies concentrations of photographed places. These distributions are then interpreted through five landscape-image elements: edge, path, district, landmark and node. Superimposing them produces a reading of the ritual route’s perceived structure.

This is evidence of photographed attention. It is not a count of all pilgrims, a complete record of sacred value or an unbiased measure of use. People who photograph and publish their journeys are selectively represented. The maps therefore help formulate spatial questions rather than settle them.
sections.caption: 01 / Edge, path, district, landmark and node. Team analysis extracted from “1227汇报.pdf”, p. 26; read with the image-density map on p. 25. Underlying photographs are social-media material, not claimed as the authors’ field photography.

sections.title: Facilities: presence, purpose and perception.
paragraphs: The facility inventory orders buildings and structures along a sacred–secular spectrum. Temples, stupas, prayer flags and mani structures are compared with inns, supply points and signs. Material, colour, use and relationship to the setting become analytical variables rather than a simple preference for one style.

The team also reports 103 returned semantic-differential questionnaires. The presentation describes more positive evaluations of religious buildings and structures, and more negative responses to some secular facilities. The scores are mapped spatially as a visual-evaluation index. This finding concerns the evaluated sample; it cannot establish approval by local religious communities or all users of the route.
sections.caption: 02 / Facility taxonomy. Hao Chang & Mengzhe Lee, “1227汇报.pdf”, p. 29. The sacred–secular and building–structure axes organise an inventory, not a ranking of religious significance.

rows: Differences in presence, material and use
Questions for siting and further investigation

sections.title: Atmosphere cannot vote on behalf of a community
paragraphs: Peter Zumthor’s Bruder Klaus chapel provides a focused comparison for reading how approach, enclosure and construction give a small building its presence. The comparison stops at that architectural question. A commissioned chapel in one religious setting cannot establish what is appropriate on the Kailash kora. [K6]

This limit matters because a restrained appearance can be mistaken for ethical restraint. A low, earth-coloured structure may still occupy a culturally sensitive place, alter a view associated with ritual or introduce servicing that changes the route. Conversely, a visually ordinary facility may provide indispensable support. Appearance, necessity and cultural authority are different forms of evidence.

The visual survey should therefore be used to generate questions rather than a league table of acceptable architecture. A negative score might relate to scale, maintenance, colour, use or placement. Without separating these factors, replacing the building with a more attractive object could preserve the actual problem.

sections.title: Perception alone cannot select a site.
paragraphs: Hydrology, terrain, slope, roads, settlements and ritual nodes are read alongside ecological conditions and geological hazards. Wildlife sightings inferred from social-media photographs are treated as provisional encounter locations, not a wildlife census. The site-selection maps overlay cultural and visual concerns with natural constraints.

The study identifies six recurring issues: protection of sacred landscape, human–wildlife interaction, pilgrim safety, inadequate supply facilities, visual disruption and geological risk. Their overlap changes the question from “where is a memorable view?” to “where can necessary care be provided with the least conflicting presence?”
sections.caption: 03 / Natural-condition overlays used in node selection. Team presentation, p. 48. These research layers guide a design test; they do not constitute an engineering hazard assessment.

sections.title: Some constraints should not be averaged away
paragraphs: Layered mapping can create an impression that every criterion is commensurable. A favourable view, gentle slope and existing path may add up to a persuasive location even when one cultural or ecological constraint should rule it out. The method needs an order of decisions, not only a composite score.

I propose beginning with exclusions established through custodial knowledge and specialist risk assessment. Within the remaining territory, compare access, servicing, existing facilities and the needs of different users. Only then should the visual and experiential qualities of a site help calibrate an intervention. The current research does not establish those exclusion boundaries; it identifies the necessity of agreeing them.

sections.title: Four degrees of architectural presence.
paragraphs: The architectural responses are tests of calibration. Distance protects spaces whose meaning or ecology should not be crowded. Adaptation improves existing support. Retention works with a footprint or relationship already present. Minimum addition addresses an essential gap without making a new landmark. These are editorial readings of the team’s siting and facility proposals.

sections.statement: Care is the method by which architecture decides whether, where and how strongly it should exist.

sections.title: Every shelter casts a service footprint
paragraphs: A remote supply station occupies more than the area under its roof. Deliveries, waste storage, wastewater, fuel, repairs and the paths used to reach it can extend its effect across the landscape. A small pavilion supplied frequently may be more demanding than an improvement to an established facility. The study must compare these chains rather than equate compactness with low impact.

The lodge, supply station and interpretation hall consequently need different operating arguments. A lodge supports sustained occupation; a supply point should answer a specific gap along the route; a hall must justify why interpretation requires a building at that location. If the same purpose can be met farther from a sensitive place, distance becomes a positive architectural decision.

The claim of care is strongest when the proposal can accept subtraction. An unsuccessful siting test should be able to remove a building, not merely make it smaller. The unbuilt option is part of the research outcome.

sections.title: Care continues after construction.
paragraphs: The study’s guidelines emphasise minimal construction, low ecological impact, restrained appearance, environmental systems and maintenance. Operation therefore belongs to the architectural question: supply, waste removal, repairs and seasonal closure can alter a facility’s footprint beyond the building itself. [K4]

Further work would need disclosed questionnaire recruitment and respondent characteristics, specialist ecology and risk studies, and consultation with religious custodians, residents and pilgrims. Neither a perception score nor a rendering proves cultural acceptance. The route’s safety and ecological integrity remain conditions to investigate, not benefits established by the proposal.

The IUCN guidance on sacred natural sites locates conservation within cultural and spiritual relationships, reinforcing the need to work with the people responsible for a place. A visually discreet building is not, by itself, evidence of culturally appropriate intervention. [K5]

title: Whose Waterfront?
proposition: Opening a route to the lake can enlarge public life and intensify pressure on the people living beside it. The design must specify whose access improves, and on what terms.
question: How can a historic waterfront become an urban seam that reconnects water, neighbourhood life, cultural memory and contemporary commerce without reducing the district to a tourist landscape?
opening: Waterfront+ begins with discontinuities around the Fire God Temple, Di’anmen and Baimi Xiejie: between water and hutongs, commercial frontages and residential space, historic landmarks and everyday routes. The research treats these breaks as different kinds of permeability to be repaired, rather than a shoreline to be opened uniformly.
credit:
Collaborative urban-design research · Hao Chang & Mengzhe Lee · 2024
Waterfront+ · Supporting academic studies are credited separately and are not the authors’ fieldwork

sections.title: Water changes its civic role.
paragraphs: The project script traces changing uses of water around the site: transport, gardens, swimming, tourist boating and winter ice activity. The relation between water and city is therefore historical and seasonal. What appears today as an edge has also been a route, a workplace, a destination and a shared civic setting.

The team’s drawings locate cultural, spatial and historical discontinuities within this changing landscape. The design problem is not simply insufficient waterfront access. It is the weakening of connections between local identity, residential life, commerce and the historic city.
sections.caption: 01 / Historical timeline extracted from Waterfront+ board 1. Hao Chang & Mengzhe Lee. The sequence is a project synthesis; the historical source literature remains separately credited.

sections.title: Different evidence answers different questions.
paragraphs: Published research by Liu Yifei and colleagues used 30 GoPro participants and extracted 25,089 images to examine visual perception along the Shichahai waterfront. Their study found stronger perception of landmarks than edges and paths, and argued for coherent views and visual corridors. These data belong to that published study; they were not collected by the Waterfront+ team. [S2]

Shao Lei’s research on resident differentiation shows why “the community” cannot be treated as one uniform constituency: economic circumstances, housing conditions and preferences for change differ. Bian Lanchun and Jing Zhongjie’s conservation work offers a complementary method, using protection frameworks and courtyard-level records and guidance. Together, these sources help distinguish visual legibility, social needs and the unit of physical intervention. [S3] [S4]

This literature informs the present research reading. It is not presented as proof that the design’s original process implemented each published method or that earlier survey findings describe current residents unchanged.

sections.title: Begin with an occupied unit, not an empty diagram
paragraphs: Zhang Ke’s Hutong Children’s Library & Art Centre provides a useful comparison because a small shared programme is placed within an inherited courtyard condition. The relevant method is close attention to what can coexist at that scale. The precedent does not demonstrate that an entire waterfront district will respond in the same way. [S5]

For Waterfront+, the courtyard is both a physical unit and a set of thresholds among people. Its entrance, circulation and shared surfaces cannot be read as vacant capacity merely because they appear open on a plan. A proposed passage may cross a place of domestic work, waiting or informal supervision. These relationships require observation and negotiation before they can become a public route.

The implication is to redraw the district as a series of differentiated permissions. Some connections can be public through-routes; others should be shared locally, open at certain times or remain private. The design gains precision when it can explain a retained boundary as clearly as a new opening.

sections.title: Four permeabilities; three publics.
paragraphs: The project’s own analysis compares urban form, transport, building character, condition, public space and programme. Cross-reading character with condition informs decisions to retain, repair, adapt, open or insert. A courtyard provides an incremental unit; linked routes and water-facing spaces allow interventions to operate at the scale of point, line and area.
The research is organised here through four kinds of permeability. They are a framework for evaluating the project drawings, not four measured performance scores.

sections.title: An opening is not yet a public relationship.
paragraphs: The combined reading suggests that physical access is necessary but insufficient. A newly opened passage may still serve only visitor consumption. A clear view of the water may coexist with a loss of affordable everyday uses. The distinction between resident-oriented, shared and visitor-oriented programmes therefore becomes central to evaluating an intervention.

The drawings propose a community library, activity centre, shared dining, public landscape and commercial interfaces. These should be judged together: do they sustain ordinary use through the day and across seasons, and do they give residents reasons to remain? Those questions extend the design beyond the number of openings along a water-facing facade.
sections.statement: The aim is not simply to bring people closer to the water, but to bring the water back into the everyday structure of the city.

sections.title: Publicness has a timetable and a cost
paragraphs: The resident returning home, the child going to an activity room and the visitor following the lake share parts of the same network but do not ask the same things of it. Their routes differ in repetition, time, speed and tolerance for crowding. A continuous promenade can improve visitor orientation while making an ordinary trip longer or noisier for a resident.

A useful evaluation therefore follows these journeys separately through the proposed plan. It asks which doors must remain open, which facilities can be reached without a purchase and which uses survive outside peak visitor hours. This is a proposed test of the design, not a claim to have measured its outcomes.

Commercial activity may finance maintenance and attract use, but it can also make free occupation conditional. The proposal’s community library, dining and activity spaces should be assessed through access rules and running costs, not only their programme labels. A room called “community” has not yet established who can book it, who can enter or who pays to keep it available.

sections.title: Waterfront+ as a sequence of repairs.
paragraphs: The project script works through existing nodes rather than a single continuous object: Yandai Xiejie, Di’anmen’s commercial block, the Fire God Temple and the Baimi Xiejie neighbourhood. Retaining useful structure, adapting courtyards, adjusting circulation and inserting shared spaces carry the waterfront into the district. The strategy diagrams connect removal and preservation, transport, public nodes and landscape views.

At the neighbourhood scale, the courtyard becomes a unit for gradual change. At the urban scale, paths and view corridors reconnect larger systems. The section tests how water-facing public life can coexist with the depth of the hutong fabric, rather than replace it with a thin tourist frontage.
sections.caption: 03 / Four linked strategies: retention and removal, transport, public nodes and view corridors. Extracted from Waterfront+ board 3; read as proposed transformations, not completed works.

sections.title: Commercial vitality without a tourist monoculture.
paragraphs: A staged renewal strategy should begin with interventions that can improve ordinary access and shared use without depending on a complete commercial redevelopment. Each stage would need a record of affected uses, conservation constraints and the people responsible for operation. The courtyard unit makes such staging imaginable; it does not remove the need to negotiate ownership and occupancy.

The project does not demonstrate that spatial improvements prevent displacement. Tenure, affordability, business continuity and the distribution of commercial benefit remain decisive. A credible assessment would compare conditions before and after each stage, including who remains and who gains access, rather than treating greater visitor activity as a sufficient measure of success.

The research conclusion is selective permeability: open the connections that support shared life, retain the thresholds that make inhabitation possible, and attach an operating commitment to every new public room.
