title: The Public Floor
proposition: Suspending a library can release the ground. Whether that ground becomes public depends on its connections, its uses and the rules that remain after the architectural gesture.
question: How can the section of a library connect urban access, collective learning and environmental systems into a continuous civic interior?
opening: Between Chang’an Avenue and the hutongs, the library study treats the section as a research instrument. Ground, suspended volumes, gardens and bridges are read together to test how a place of knowledge can remain connected to the city through movement, shared use and environmental exchange.
credit:
Collaborative studio and design research · Hao Chang & Mengzhe Lee · 2024
Hao’s role: lead concept, diagrams, modelling and sections · Instructor: Martijn de Geus

sections.title: The institution and the ground it occupies.
paragraphs: The portfolio frames the site through the relationship between Chang’an Avenue and the hutongs. A library here is not only a destination for readers. Its edge and ground floor affect how different urban conditions meet. The study asks whether the institution can provide a shared route and civic room as well as a collection of interior programmes.

The enquiry uses urban analysis, sectional drawings and physical models to test spatial relationships. The IFLA–UNESCO Public Library Manifesto offers an institutional frame: the library’s public purpose extends across education, culture, information and inclusion. Architecture must turn that ambition into accessible rooms, routes and usable time. [B2]

sections.title: From the common hall to the metropolitan interior
paragraphs: Hertzberger describes the classrooms of the Delft Montessori school as identifiable places along a shared hall. The comparison helps distinguish collective space from an undifferentiated open plan: people need a place from which to participate, as well as a space in which to meet. [B3]

Applied to the library, this suggests examining the edges between reading, circulation, discussion and retreat. A large continuous interior can be visually democratic while making it difficult to concentrate or to occupy a place without feeling exposed. Publicness requires options at different scales: the individual seat, the small group, the shared route and the institution as a whole.

The research therefore reads the section as a set of invitations and separations. A bridge is more than a connection if it offers somewhere to pause without obstructing movement. A garden contributes to shared use only if its approach, seating and maintenance allow it to be occupied. These relationships can be tested without assuming that maximum openness is always desirable.

sections.title: Read one section through four systems.
paragraphs: The sectional perspective is examined successively as space, structure, climate and programme. Each reading asks what enables or interrupts continuity. Physical models test the relation between suspended volumes, support, light and the ground plane. This shared section makes the systems comparable without pretending they operate independently.
sections.caption: 01 / Section as a common analytical frame. Hao Chang & Mengzhe Lee, Books Above Bustles. The drawing is used to compare spatial, structural, climatic and programmatic relationships.

rows: How do rooms and routes connect?
Gardens and bridges link a vertical public interior
What can remain open beneath occupied volumes?
Suspended volumes and spanning support free parts of the ground
How do roof, envelope and interior exchange resources?
Solar systems, ventilation and water capture are considered together
Where do different forms of learning overlap?
Reading, education, exhibition and shared rooms meet along a social spine

sections.title: Civic continuity has a vertical dimension.
paragraphs: The section suggests that public space need not stop at the ground floor. Bridges, gardens and reading areas extend the possibility of shared occupation upward. The architectural finding is a proposition about continuity: different rooms can contribute to a public institution when the routes between them are treated as meaningful civic space.

Continuity is more demanding than visual openness. A route must also be understandable, accessible and usable under the institution’s operating rules. The drawings establish a spatial possibility; they do not establish equal access, freedom from exclusion or a particular pattern of use.
sections.statement: The civic value of a room depends partly on the relationships that make it accessible.

sections.title: Follow the person who did not come for a book
paragraphs: A civic library also receives someone seeking a quiet place, a meeting, information or a route through the district. To test the public floor, I trace an arrival from the street through entry, orientation, vertical movement and a destination. The chain is only as accessible as its most restrictive threshold. A generous room at the top cannot compensate for an uncertain entrance below.

This reading distinguishes an urban shortcut from admission to the institution. They may share a ground plane while requiring different hours and degrees of supervision. The design should make that boundary explicit, so that closing a reading area does not unnecessarily close the common route. The drawings suggest a spatial opportunity; the operating brief would have to secure it.

A second chain follows a person who cannot use the prominent stair. Equivalent access involves more than providing a lift somewhere in the building. It includes legibility, distance, continuity and arrival at the same civic places. These are criteria for the next design test, not certified results of the present scheme.

sections.title: Structure makes a public promise.
paragraphs: Suspending volumes changes the relation between occupied space and the city below. The truss and modular grid are therefore studied as civic decisions as well as structural ones: they influence which parts of the ground can remain permeable and how shared interiors meet across the section.

The physical model provides a second reading of that promise. It tests the proximity of volumes, the depth of light and the experience of openings. Its value is comparative and spatial; load paths, movement, fire strategy and long-span feasibility would need separate technical verification.
sections.caption: 02 / Physical model as a spatial test. Project team, 2024. Suspended masses and their intervening spaces are examined together.

sections.title: Learning space as an environmental relationship.
paragraphs: Roof energy systems, cross-atrium ventilation, an adaptive envelope, rainwater capture and interior gardens are located within the same sectional argument. The environmental systems are not presented as a separate list of sustainable features: the study asks how they shape places for reading, movement and gathering.

This coupling creates an architectural question rather than a proven efficiency claim. Ventilation and daylight may support public occupation in one part of the building while producing heat, glare or acoustic conflicts elsewhere. The section makes those dependencies available for testing.

sections.title: A system drawing must also show disagreement
paragraphs: The four readings of the section are most useful where they conflict. An atrium may connect floors while transmitting noise. A glazed edge can admit daylight and produce glare. A planted interior needs water and maintenance routes beside places intended for books and sustained concentration. Suspending a volume opens space below while increasing the demands on structure and servicing.

Rather than presenting those systems as automatically complementary, the research identifies the interfaces that require a choice. Which reading areas need acoustic separation? Where should shading protect occupation? Can garden maintenance occur without closing the public route? The architectural argument becomes stronger when its celebrated sectional continuity can survive these ordinary demands.

sections.title: A public building needs an operating model.
paragraphs: The unresolved questions include universal access, opening hours, security thresholds, acoustic separation, wayfinding and the maintenance of shared gardens and environmental systems. None can be answered by a sectional image alone.

The next stage would compare the proposal against access scenarios, environmental simulation and institutional requirements. This study contributes an integrated way of asking those questions: collective knowledge depends on the spaces between programmes, the support beneath them and the rules through which people can use them.

title: Culture After the Ribbon-Cutting
proposition: The opening of a cultural building is one event. Its civic value is made repeatedly through access, tenancy, maintenance and the freedom of people to use the spaces around it.
question: How do architecture, development and everyday stewardship produce a cultural ecosystem?
opening: I joined the third Bi-City Youth Cultural Leadership Programme expecting to learn about museums and cultural institutions. The experience expanded into a question about how culture is produced by a city. Encounters with Swire Properties were especially influential: they made the decisions between design and daily life—management, programming, tenancy, maintenance and public access—part of my architectural enquiry.
credit:
Field reflection and urban research · Hao Chang · 2024
Third Bi-City Youth Cultural Leadership Programme
Organised by Hong Kong Palace Museum · Lead sponsor: Swire Properties

sections.title: Culture depends on relationships.
paragraphs: The 2024 programme brought sixteen university students from Hong Kong and Beijing into a two-month exchange across Hong Kong, Chengdu and Beijing under the theme “The Future of Cultural Ecosystems.” Workshops, visits and institutional encounters placed different forms of cultural production in relation. [H1]

Hong Kong became the principal territory of my reflection. A museum needs audiences, educators, public space and infrastructure; a neighbourhood depends on businesses, residents and accumulated memories. A place to gather needs maintenance and repeated occupation. The word ecosystem becomes useful when it shifts attention from an isolated cultural object to the relationships that allow it to act in the city.

sections.title: The developer as an urban actor.
paragraphs: My exchanges with Swire Properties challenged a narrow understanding of developers as actors who finance and deliver buildings. The programme presented placemaking as an ongoing relationship among art, local culture, development and management. Swire’s published account makes this institutional ambition explicit. [H2]

For me, the important shift was temporal. An architect may be involved through a defined period of design and delivery; an owner or developer may continue shaping a district for decades. Tenant selection, access rules, landscape care and cultural programming can change the meaning of a place as profoundly as its initial plan. Development therefore becomes a subject of architectural research, rather than only a condition outside it.

sections.title: Control can be mapped as carefully as circulation
paragraphs: The encounter with development practice changed the scale of the brief for me. Instead of ending with a completed space, I began tracing the decisions that continually produce it: who selects tenants, approves events, maintains planting, changes opening hours and responds to a conflict over use. These decisions do not necessarily belong to the same actor.

A spatially continuous district can therefore contain discontinuous rights. Walking across a plaza, remaining there and organising an activity may be governed differently. A future study should map those permissions beside the pedestrian network. This would allow generous physical provision and restrictive use rules to be assessed together, rather than assuming one cancels out the other.

The comparison with ordinary neighbourhood space is not a claim that unmanaged conditions are automatically more inclusive. Informal territories also have exclusions and hierarchies. The question is whether people can understand, negotiate and influence the rules through which either kind of space operates.

sections.title: A generous plaza raises questions of control.
paragraphs: At developments such as Taikoo Place, I began asking how the project meets the existing city and what happens between buildings. Can someone remain without shopping? Can a small cultural organisation participate? How does a place change over time, and who decides which activities belong there?

A privately governed space can support substantial public life while retaining rules that shape access and expression. That tension is not resolved by an attractive ground floor or the presence of public art. It calls for a more precise account of publicness: who can enter, who can stay, who can organise an activity and who can contest a decision.

rows: When is it open, and under whose rules?
Who can programme it or use it informally?

sections.title: Walking beyond the curated development.
paragraphs: Neighbourhood streets and housing estates offered a counterpoint to professional placemaking. Corridors, podiums, markets and small shops showed how use accumulates through repeated ordinary decisions. A designed framework is continually interpreted by the people who inhabit it.

Walking became a way to examine transitions rather than collect landmarks: station to shopping centre, housing estate to market, temple to infrastructure, old neighbourhood to redevelopment. The question was what connects these settings and which forms of everyday life are supported at their edges. This reading does not turn every informal use into an ideal; it asks what a managed project can learn from continuity that it did not centrally design.

sections.title: Draw a situation rather than a landmark
paragraphs: Atelier Bow-Wow’s research, including Made in Tokyo and Pet Architecture, examines urban combinations that conventional building categories can overlook. I use this as a comparative method for attending to relationships between use and setting. It sharpens the Hong Kong reflection without recasting a personal walk as a completed ethnographic survey. [H3]

The research unit becomes a recurring situation: someone waiting where a passage widens, a shop edge that supports conversation, a route between a housing estate and a market. Its drawing would include the activity, physical support, time and governing rule. The same bench can support a brief pause, a daily meeting or a managed event; the difference lies partly beyond its form.

Repetition matters because an exceptional festival and an ordinary weekday reveal different capacities. A proper next stage would revisit selected transitions at comparable times and record what changes. The present reflection identifies those situations as questions; it does not supply invented counts, interviews or claims about all residents.

sections.title: Chengdu and Beijing sharpened the question.
paragraphs: The programme’s Chengdu visits connected cultural institutions with Taikoo Li Chengdu and its relationship to the Daci Temple. The official account identifies heritage, art and commercial development as explicit subjects of the exchange. [H1] [H2]

The resulting question for me was what preservation retains: fabric, urban morphology, cultural practices, memory or an image of history. Beijing shifted the frame toward institutional conservation and the communication of heritage. Hong Kong remained the place where I could bring these scales back together, because institutions, commerce, infrastructure and neighbourhood life are so closely interwoven.

sections.title: From a cultural ecosystem to a shared record.
paragraphs: Their Story, the Eastern District community calendar, provided a smaller scale for this enquiry. Local stories become material that can be edited, designed and circulated, asking whose everyday experience is visible within the public image of a place. The project extends architectural attention from built form to cultural representation.

A printed calendar cannot stand in for a neighbourhood or resolve its competing interests. Its value lies in making specific stories available for shared attention. It also places responsibility on the editor: selection and presentation should remain attentive to the people represented.
sections.caption: Their Story · Eastern District community calendar project. Field research and a shared cultural record developed in the Bi-City programme context.

sections.title: Who gets to become the story of a place?
paragraphs: A community calendar makes this question tangible. Editorial selection gives some experiences visibility and leaves others outside the frame. The design work must distinguish a person’s account from the editor’s interpretation, and an individual story from a claim about a whole neighbourhood. The calendar is a situated cultural object, not a substitute for collective representation.

This brings the larger discussion of placemaking back to a modest scale. Cultural value is not produced only by commissioning prominent art or programming an event. It also depends on the means through which people can describe their own place, disagree with its public image and keep a record that lasts beyond a campaign. Stewardship includes who can revise that record.

sections.title: Design continues through stewardship.
paragraphs: The most consequential change in my thinking was to look at actors and time alongside space. Urban quality depends on a continuing process of adaptation, programming, investment and care. Culture can shape development early, but it can also become branding if the ability of people to participate is left unexamined.

I now approach a project with a larger set of questions: who owns and manages it, who uses it, who remembers what was there before and what happens after the opening photographs. The enquiry remains deliberately open about the relationship between commercial value and cultural value. The task is to make their negotiation visible and ask how it can become more inclusive.
sections.statement: Architecture creates space; stewardship shapes what a place can continue to become.
